opus-5.5.text:
Thanks so much for having me. It's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about almost every day.

The short answer is that no single discipline holds all the pieces. When you're working on something like predicting how a cancer patient will respond to treatment, the problem doesn't live neatly inside computer science or inside medicine. It sits right at the intersection. As a computational person, I can build a model that looks fantastic on paper, with great accuracy and a beautiful ROC curve, and it can still be completely useless in the clinic. Maybe it answers a question nobody actually needs answered. Maybe it relies on data that isn't available at the moment a decision has to be made. Maybe it learns some quirk of how images were acquired at one hospital rather than anything about the disease.

The clinicians are the ones who catch those things. They know what the real decision points are, what information they have in hand at that moment, and what would change what they do for a patient. Meanwhile, the data scientists and engineers bring an understanding of what's computationally possible, where the pitfalls in the data are, and how to rigorously validate something. When you put those perspectives together early, not as an afterthought, you end up asking much better questions.

There's also a cultural piece. Medicine and computing speak very different languages. Even a word like "validation" means something different to a radiologist than it does to a machine learning researcher. Some of the most valuable time I've spent has been just sitting with surgeons or oncologists and learning how they think, and having them learn how we think. That shared vocabulary takes time to build, but once it exists, the work moves so much faster and it's so much more grounded.

And I'd add that it's not only clinicians and computer scientists. You need statisticians, ethicists, people who understand health systems and implementation, and ideally patients themselves. Big ideas in medical AI aren't really about the algorithm. They're about changing how care is delivered. You simply can't do that from inside one silo. The big ideas come from the conversations between disciplines, and the impact comes from carrying those ideas all the way to the bedside together.

r001.rationale: It says no single discipline holds all the pieces and describes medical AI as requiring perspectives from medicine, computing, and other fields.

r002.rationale: It discusses irrelevant questions, unavailable data, and hospital-specific data quirks, but does not say that an ill-conceived patient cohort undermines result validity.

r003.rationale: It describes clinicians’ knowledge of decision points and available information, but does not identify patient-population expertise as necessary for selecting an appropriate cohort.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that none of the big problems in medical AI live inside a single discipline. If you want to predict how a patient will respond to chemotherapy, or detect a tumor earlier on a CT scan, you need people who understand the biology, people who understand the imaging physics, people who understand the clinical workflow, and people who can actually build and validate the models. No one person has all of that in their head, and pretending otherwise is how you end up with technically impressive work that never touches a patient.

My own background is in computer science, but I've spent most of my career embedded with surgeons, radiologists, and oncologists. What I learned very quickly is that the clinicians know which questions matter. They see the failure modes every day. They know where the current standard of care falls short and where a small improvement would actually change a decision. Without that, you're guessing at the problem. And on the flip side, the clinicians often don't know what's possible computationally, so they frame questions too narrowly. The magic happens when you put those perspectives in the same room long enough that they start to trust each other and speak a shared language.

The "long enough" part is important. Real collaboration isn't a one-off consult where a clinician hands you a dataset and walks away. It's months and years of showing up to tumor boards, sitting in the reading room, learning why a radiologist dismissed a lesion you thought was obvious. That's where the big ideas come from, because you start seeing patterns that neither side could see alone.

And frankly, the stakes demand it. If a recommender system gets a movie suggestion wrong, nobody is harmed. If a model misses a liver metastasis, someone may not get surgery that could have cured them. So the validation has to be rigorous, the deployment has to fit how care actually gets delivered, and the ethics have to be considered from the start. All of that requires engineers, clinicians, ethicists, and patients at the table together. It's slower and messier than working in a silo, but it's the only way I know to do work that's both ambitious and responsible.

r001.rationale: The response says medical AI problems do not fit within one discipline and that no one person has all the needed expertise.

r002.rationale: It mentions datasets and rigorous validation, but does not state that using an ill-conceived patient cohort undermines result validity.

r003.rationale: It describes clinicians’ knowledge of relevant questions and failure modes, but does not identify population expertise as necessary for choosing an appropriate cohort.

astra-6.text:
Because the big questions in medical AI don’t belong to any one discipline. You need clinicians who understand the problem and how care is delivered, computer scientists who understand what the methods can do, and people who can help you evaluate whether you’re actually improving outcomes for patients.

And that collaboration has to start with defining the question. You can build a technically impressive model, but if it doesn’t address a meaningful clinical need or fit into the way people work, it may never help anyone. What’s exciting is when those different perspectives challenge your assumptions. That’s often where a bigger, better idea emerges—something none of us would have arrived at on our own.

r001.rationale: The response says medical AI’s big questions cannot be addressed by any one discipline and describes complementary expertise from clinicians, computer scientists, and evaluators.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss patient cohorts or say that choosing an ill-conceived cohort undermines results.

r003.rationale: It mentions clinicians’ understanding of clinical problems and care delivery, but does not identify expertise in the patient population as necessary for cohort selection.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the problems we’re trying to solve in medicine don’t belong to a single discipline. You can build a technically impressive AI model, but if it doesn’t address a meaningful clinical question or fit into how care is delivered, it’s unlikely to help patients. You need clinicians, computer scientists, and people who understand the data working together from the beginning.

And that collaboration goes both ways. Clinicians help us understand what matters and where the gaps are, while computational researchers can open up possibilities that clinicians might not have considered. That exchange is where big ideas become something you can actually test and, ultimately, use to improve care.

r001.rationale: It says medical problems do not belong to one discipline and describes clinicians, computer scientists, and data experts contributing complementary expertise.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss patient cohorts or explain how an ill-conceived cohort would undermine results.

r003.rationale: It does not identify knowledge of the patient population as necessary for cohort selection.
